title: The boy in the temple (Luke 2:41–52)
hook: twelve-year-old Jesus goes missing for three days and is found asking questions
tomorrow: The wild man by the river

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flight into Egypt and the Holy Innocents: a family running by night. He was a refugee first.

A crowded store. A parent turns around, and the child isn't there. Now stretch that moment to three days. Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem for Passover, and this year Jesus is twelve. When the feast ends they start home with a big group of relatives and neighbors, assuming he's somewhere in the crowd. A whole day's walk later they look for him, and he's gone. They turn back. Three days of searching a packed city.
screen: `WHERE'S THE KID?` → `A WHOLE DAY'S WALK.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: They find him in the temple courts, "sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. He isn't lecturing them. He's listening, and asking, and everyone who hears him is astonished at his understanding and his answers. Then Mary speaks, in the voice of a frightened parent: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." The boy's answer is the first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" A small puzzle: the Greek is short and can be read two ways, my Father's business or my Father's house. Translators still choose between them. Either way, his first words point to God as his Father. And his parents, Luke says plainly, didn't understand. He goes home with them and is obedient to them, and Mary, again, keeps all these sayings in her heart. The four Gospels tell no other story from the years between his infancy and his adult life. Years of silence, and the one scene we're given is a boy asking questions in the house of God. Then one line for everything after: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." Even he grew, a little at a time.
screen: `FOUND AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `HEARING THEM, AND ASKING THEM.` · `MY FATHER'S BUSINESS, OR HOUSE?` · `NO OTHER STORY FROM THOSE YEARS.` · then, large: `JESUS INCREASED IN WISDOM AND STATURE.`

segments.voice: Look for a question you've been carrying, about God, about your life, about something you were taught that never quite made sense: a real one, not a polite one. Some people hide their questions because they think faith means having answers, but the boy in this story sits in the temple asking, so say yours to yourself plainly, in one sentence. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is.
Doctors. The King James word for the temple scholars, the teachers of the law that twelve-year-old Jesus sat among, listening and asking questions.
Your line: questions belong in the temple. Tomorrow, a wild man by the river, and the grown-up years begin. That's day forty-six.

screen: `DAY 46 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WILD MAN BY THE RIVER.`

howItsDone: Many churches read this story in the Christmas season, and Catholics pray it as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the temple. Christian art often shows the boy seated among the teachers.

fork.setup: you're Mary. after three days you find your son among the teachers in the temple. what do you say?
options: nothing. just hug him and leave.
son, why have you done this to us? we searched for you, sorrowing.
scold him in front of everyone.
fork.reveal: Mary asks why, and says his father and she sought him sorrowing. his answer, about his Father's business, is the first thing Jesus says in Luke.

original.note: Greek: teacher. Luke finds the boy in the midst of the teachers; later, people will call him teacher too.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a clever child showing off.
what it means: a boy listening and asking questions in the house of God, and parents who don't yet understand.
what a scholar hears: his first words in Luke, en tois tou patros mou, can mean my Father's business or my Father's house, and translators still choose between them.

notes: 'The first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel' — Luke 2:49 is his first recorded speech in Luke; confirm.
Luke 2:49 Greek ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου is ambiguous ('my Father's house' or 'my Father's affairs'); KJV has 'business'.

'The only story in the four Gospels from the years between infancy and adult life' refers to the canonical Gospels (later non-canonical infancy gospels exist). 'Eighteen years or so' assumes Luke 3:23 ('about thirty years of age'); confirm.
The script avoids calling this a bar mitzvah (a later custom, at thirteen).
Finding in the Temple is the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary; confirm.
